name: Hana Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Hana, thanks for joining. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech firms, employers or government. Everything you say here is confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working week looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I'm in my bedroom studio making short tracks for a stock music library, the kind of thing people put under cooking videos and podcast intros. I get paid a few pounds each time someone licenses one. Two evenings a week I play keyboard in the pit band for the amateur theatre in town, and I'm halfway through a musical about a lighthouse right now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that I can finish a track at 2am and someone in another country uses it by breakfast. I use AI tools every day, for chord ideas, mastering, writing my track descriptions. The hard part is that I'm not a great mixer yet, and my income jumps around. Last month was 610 pounds, the month before was 340, and I have about ten days of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a nice set of tools, not a replacement, and that's what I always said. I'd post a little video showing my setup. Other producers would argue in the comments, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because the stock library pays less every year anyway. There are millions of tracks and the price per licence keeps dropping. Even small AI tools let people with no training upload hundreds of tracks, and that floods my corner of the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to work faster, aiming for ten finished tracks a week instead of six. I'd ask the theatre if they need a keyboard player for the Christmas panto too. And I'd try to land a couple of direct jingle jobs for local businesses so I'm less dependent on the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Not scared, but I'd still check my earnings page every morning, and it still makes my chest tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the price per licence keeps falling. How much does a track earn you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago a good track made me maybe 40 pounds over a year. Now it's more like 15. I'm running faster to stay in the same place, and the rent went up 50 pounds in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the local jingle work look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery on the high street wants a little tune for their radio advert, and the driving school asked my mum about something similar. It's maybe 150 pounds a job, which is ten tracks' worth of library money. I'd be happy to do jingles all day if they kept coming.

say: AI became a **nice set of tools**, not a replacement.
She'd post a **setup video**, and producers would argue in the comments.
think: Stock library pay **falls every year**, AI hype or not.
Even small tools let beginners **flood the market** with tracks.
do: Use AI to finish **ten tracks** a week instead of six.
Ask the theatre about **Christmas panto** work.
Find **direct jingle** jobs for local businesses.
feel: **Restless**, with a **tight chest** every morning on the earnings page.
S0.quote: Two years ago a good track made me maybe 40 pounds over a year. Now it's more like 15.
fieldNote: Her income is **already shrinking** from flooded stock libraries.
She uses AI **every day** and sees it as a speed tool.
Local **jingle work** pays ten times better and is her escape route.

steps.text: Use AI tools to finish ten library tracks a week
Ask the theatre for the Christmas panto keyboard job
Pitch radio jingles to the bakery and driving school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Online I'd say AI firms owe musicians, because they trained on our work for free. I'd push for a law that says AI music has to be labelled. I'd also say, honestly, that people like me have to change how we work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the stock library is finished for me. If a video maker can type 'cosy cooking music' and get a track in ten seconds, nobody licenses mine. That's most of my income. The theatre pit is safer, because amateur theatres want a real person with a real keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd stop uploading to the library and put that time into live work: theatre pits, wedding ceremonies, a piano bar if one exists. I'd sell AI-assisted custom music to local firms as a service, where the human part is me listening to what they want. I'd also look at moving to the city, where there are ten theatres instead of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm losing the thing I built, but also weirdly awake. I'd be sad for a week and then start making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be selling AI-made music while your main work disappears to AI. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I think about it too long. But my landlord doesn't take principles as rent. I'd be clear with customers about what's AI and what's me, and I'd still campaign for artists to be paid for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to the city cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Higher rent, maybe 200 pounds more a month, and losing the theatre people, who are basically my family here. I'd need to save at least a month's rent first, which I've never managed. I'd probably sublet a room from a friend first, to test it.

say: AI firms **owe musicians** for training on their work.
AI music should be **labelled** by law.
People like her must **change how they work**.
think: The **stock library** is finished for her, and it's most of her income.
The **theatre pit** is safer because shows want a live player.
do: Stop library uploads and shift to **live work**.
Sell **custom music** to local firms, using AI for speed.
Test a **move to the city** by subletting from a friend.
feel: **Loss** for a week, then **wide awake** and making lists.
S1.quote: My landlord doesn't take principles as rent.
fieldNote: She expects her **main income** to vanish in this picture.
Her principles and her **pragmatism** pull against each other.
A city move is her bold plan, held back by **no savings**.

steps.text: Stop library uploads and chase theatre and ceremony gigs
Sell AI-assisted custom jingles to local businesses
Sublet a friend's room in the city to test moving
Campaign for a law to label AI music

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency and the government should pay people while it sorts itself out. I'd join whatever musicians' group was organising. Online I'd stop arguing and start sharing practical help, like where to get emergency grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 any music made at a desk is free. That's my bedroom studio, gone. What's left is hands-on: playing a keyboard in a room full of people. That's maybe three more years until robots, and I'm not even the best keyboard player in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get every live gig I can, and I'd take lessons to get my sight-reading up so I'm the pit player theatres call first. I'd sell my studio monitors and the good microphone, maybe 900 pounds, to make a cushion. And I'd look at work that's hands-on and people-heavy, like running music sessions in care homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened but busy. I'd cope by doing, because sitting still would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With thinking AI first and robots three years later, how do you use those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd treat them as my window to become someone who's needed in the room. Care homes, schools, theatres, places where a real person matters. Music therapy needs a degree I don't have, but music sessions for older people don't always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, then Ines, the director at the theatre. Ines knows every care home manager in town from fundraising. I'd ask her straight out who might want a keyboard player on weekday afternoons.

say: This is a **public emergency**; the government should pay people.
She'd share **practical help** like emergency grants online.
think: By 2028 any **desk-made music** is free, so her studio is gone.
Live keyboard buys **three years** until robots, and she's not the best.
do: Grab every **live gig** and improve her **sight-reading**.
Sell **studio gear** for about 900 pounds as a cushion.
feel: **Frightened but busy**; doing keeps the fear down.
S2.quote: By 2028 any music made at a desk is free. That's my bedroom studio, gone.
fieldNote: She clearly sees her **desk work** goes first and her playing three years later.
Selling gear for a cushion shows **adaptive** instincts under pressure.
She leans on **local networks** like the theatre director for leads.

steps.text: Sell the studio monitors and microphone for about 900 pounds
Take sight-reading lessons to win more pit work
Ask Ines (the theatre director) for care home contacts
Join the musicians' group pushing for emergency pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to make sure musicians land somewhere. Fund community music, pay artists for training data. I'd help organise a co-op of local players so we can share bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can switch on my own terms, not in a panic. The library money fades over the first couple of years and I'd plan for that. My real worry is that I'm still learning, and I need to get good fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a community music leader course, the cheaper kind, one weekend a month. I'd set up the co-op with three or four players from the theatre. And I'd use AI hard right now to squeeze the last good money from library tracks while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but hopeful. Five years feels like I can actually steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI to squeeze the library while campaigning against unpaid training. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know it. I'd still do both. I'm not going to starve to prove a point, and the campaign is about the future, not my rent this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One shared booking page, one phone number, and fair pay rules so nobody undercuts. If a school wants a band for a leavers' party, we send whoever's free. A musicians' co-op is old-fashioned, really, like a union with a diary.

say: We have **five years** to make sure musicians land somewhere.
Fund **community music** and pay artists for training data.
She'd help start a **local co-op** of players.
think: Five years lets her switch **on her own terms**.
Her real worry is **skill**: she's still learning and must improve fast.
do: Start a **community music leader** course, one weekend a month.
Set up a **booking co-op** with theatre players.
Use AI to squeeze the **last library money**.
feel: **Nervous but hopeful**; she feels she can **steer**.
S3.quote: A musicians' co-op is old-fashioned, really, like a union with a diary.
fieldNote: She openly owns the **contradiction** of using AI while campaigning on it.
The co-op idea mixes **progressive values** with practical booking.
Income still **fades**, so worry stays despite her plan.

steps.text: Enrol on a weekend community music leader course
Set up a booking co-op with three theatre players
Use AI to finish more library tracks while they still sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, so there's no excuse for leaving artists behind. I'd keep pushing on labelling and pay. I'd also tell younger musicians to learn to play live, not just produce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a career. I could become a decent community music leader and a solid pit player by then. The library money still fades, though, so the next few years are still tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the community music course and start running a weekly session at the youth centre. I'd move into the city within two years, once I've saved, because that's where the theatres are. I'd keep using AI for the boring admin and to practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. There's still the knot about rent, because that doesn't depend on AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the library money fades either way. When do you think that bites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably within two years. That's why the ten-year picture isn't calm for me. The end point is far away, but my rent is close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the move to the city happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A month's rent saved, a couple of regular pit jobs lined up and a room with a friend. I'd give myself until I'm 29. If it doesn't work by then, I come home and teach.

say: A decade is plenty, so there's **no excuse** for leaving artists behind.
Young musicians should **learn to play live**, not just produce.
think: Ten years is a **career** as a music leader and pit player.
Library money still **fades** within two years, so the near term is tight.
do: Run a **weekly session** at the youth centre after her course.
Move to the **city** within two years once she has savings.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a **rent knot** that doesn't depend on AGI.
S4.quote: The end point is far away, but my rent is close.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, her **near-term income** keeps her anxious.
She sets a clear **deadline**: age 29 for the city move.
Teaching is her **safety net** if the city plan fails.

steps.text: Start a weekly music session at the youth centre
Save a month's rent before moving to the city
Move to the city by 29 if two pit jobs line up
Keep using AI for admin and practice drills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole studio becomes worthless before I'm good enough at anything else. What would help is a bridge: a year of basic pay while you retrain, and real money for community music, so the people who want to play with older folks or kids can get paid for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people how much they already use AI. I use it every day and I'm still worried. Being good with the AI tools doesn't make you safe, it just makes you see it coming sooner.

headlineQuote: Being good with the AI tools doesn't make you safe, it just makes you see it coming sooner.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old producer** making stock library music and playing keys in a theatre pit.
She uses **AI daily**, earns between 340 and 610 pounds a month and has ten days' rent saved.
Her **library income** already falls every year, so even AI Plateau leaves her anxious.
She moves fast: **selling gear**, chasing live work and starting a booking co-op.
Her plan B is **community music** in care homes and youth centres, or a city move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her studio becomes worthless before her skills catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A **year of basic pay** while she retrains.
